title: Concurrency and synchronization: races, locks, atomic instructions and barriers
transcript_provenance: Local machine transcription (faster-whisper small.en); not publisher captions
source_uncertainties: Peterson (1981) could not be opened (closed access). The algorithm is the textbook form; lock_model.py tests that form. Proofs of progress and bounded waiting are not given.

Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani (1971) could not be opened (access blocked). The attribution of the four conditions rests on the bibliographic record (Crossref) and on the Wikipedia article Deadlock (computer science), opened 2026-10-26.
Dijkstra EWD123 is a scanned typescript without a text layer; typescript pages 10 to 18 were read as page images. Later pages (semaphores) were not read.

Stallings (Operating Systems) and Silberschatz (Operating System Concepts, 9th ed.) are credited on the slides and were not opened; the slide code of test_and_set and compare_and_swap was read from frames f0052 to f0060; f0061 and f0062 (atomics, semaphore title) were also viewed. A statement about threads waiting in a queue appears only in the speech and not on a slide, so the chapter does not discuss it as a lecture claim.

The Intel article of Tian and Shih returned HTTP 403 to a script; it was read from the Internet Archive snapshot of 2019-07-22. The figure on the slide (f0030, f0032) is the figure the article calls Figure 3.

The chapter does not attribute the verbal explanation of the test-and-set and compare-and-swap loops to the lecturer: the machine transcript of that passage does not match the slide code, and machine transcription may have misheard it. The chapter follows the slide code.

N1570 is a committee draft, not the published standard; printed page = PDF page - 18. OpenMP 5.2 printed page = PDF page - 20; MCS page numbers (30, 33-34) and the Chandy-Lamport page (64) are derived from the position in the PDF. POSIX pages are the online Issue 7 (2018) pages.
MPI and CUDA documentation were not opened; the statements about them in the section on frameworks are pointers to other chapters.
Intel ARK was not re-opened for this chapter; the hybrid-core facts are taken from the citation in chapter 11.

Explanations given as hypotheses and not tested: (a) the higher cost per shared update of the mutex at batch sizes 10 and 100 than at 1 (sleeping and waking through the kernel, or cache-line transfers; strace -c was not run); (b) the collapse of the test-and-set spinlock from 8 threads on (descheduling of the lock holder); (c) the plateau of lock throughput at 8 and 12 threads (processor layout); (d) why four racing threads are no faster than one thread; (e) why an uncontended atomic RMW adds no measurable time in the loop (overlap with the multiply chain).

All timings come from one machine (hybrid i5-12450H, WSL 2), one compiler (gcc 13.3) and one session, with other jobs present and no control of thread placement; each timing is the minimum of 3 repetitions in one run. Ranges quoted as earlier runs (six totals of the racing counter, store-buffering rates of 7.4 to 14.1 %, Peterson overlaps of 1.7 to 2.4 % of entries, barrier ranges) come from earlier sessions of the same or earlier versions of the programs and are not reproduced by a listing. The test-and-test-and-set measurements of exercise 6 are one run of a modified counter.c that is not a listing.

An earlier draft of the store-buffering harness used a run-time memory order and observed no violation; gcc compiles a non-constant memory order as seq_cst (xchg). The listings use a constant order through macros.

ThreadSanitizer needed 'setarch x86_64 -R' under the WSL 2 kernel (it aborted with 'unexpected memory mapping' otherwise). The tsan_demo.c fragment is not a code_lab listing because the tool exits with a nonzero code on a reported race.
Timestamps are section anchors from local speech-recognition segment times and locate topic changes to within a few seconds.
lecture_corrections: Concurrency defined as several tasks on one core by time slicing: refined to the schedule model (two events are concurrent when neither happens before the other).
A race occurs when two threads access a variable at the same time: refined; a conflict without order suffices, and the slide's second schedule has no overlap.

Shared-cache figure: the handwritten annotation reads panels (A) and (B) as CPU 1 and CPU 2 and the slide puts the variable in the shared cache; in the source article they are two update policies for one pair of threads, and a shared variable lives in memory (frames f0030, f0032, f0034).
Critical section 'should not be interrupted by any other thread' (slide f0041): refined to exclusion, not non-preemption.
Mutex as a 0/1 variable set to 0 to acquire (slide f0049): needs the test and the change as one indivisible step; check-then-set fails in 6 steps in the model.
Atomics as instructions that execute without any interruption (slide f0052): refined to indivisibility with respect to other threads.
Barrier for checkpointing (slide f0067): sufficient, not necessary (Chandy and Lamport 1985).
'Higher performance can never be at the cost of accuracy' (slide f0072): true with a definition of accuracy that allows rounding differences.
